title: The voice in the desert (Matthew 3:1–12)
hook: John the Baptist in camel hair, eating locusts, calling people to turn around

segments.voice: Yesterday: tekton, the builder's trade, and eighteen quiet years in Nazareth. Today the quiet ends with a shout from the desert.

Out past the towns, in the dry country near the Jordan River, a man is shouting. He wears a rough garment of camel's hair with a leather belt. He eats locusts and wild honey. No house, no title, no invitation. And people come, Matthew says, from Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan. They stand in the river, confess their sins, and he baptizes them. This is John, the one Christians call the Baptist, a relative of Jesus. His message fits in one breath.
screen: `A MAN SHOUTING IN THE DESERT.` → `CAMEL HAIR, LOCUSTS, WILD HONEY.` → `AND THE CROWDS COME.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims Bible, the old Catholic English translation: "Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." The King James says repent. Both reach for one Greek word, metanoia. Meta, after or beyond. Noia, from the word for mind. A change of mind, a turning around. Not feeling bad, first of all: a new direction. The Douay-Rheims followed the Latin Bible's do penance, and that wording is one reason Catholics speak of the sacrament of penance: confession carries an echo of this call. Matthew hears John in the prophet Isaiah, centuries earlier: "A voice of one crying in the desert, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." Isaiah pictures a road made ready for a king: low places filled, hills brought down, the crooked made straight. John's message: a king is coming, and the road is you. He isn't gentle about it. When religious leaders come to watch, he tells them to bring forth fruit worthy of penance, to show the turning in how they live. The axe, he says, is already at the root of the trees. But he points away from himself. Someone mightier is coming after him, and John isn't worthy even to carry his sandals. The Church keeps John close. His voice fills the Sundays of Advent, and both his birth, on June twenty-fourth, and his death have their own feasts.
screen: `DO PENANCE: THE KINGDOM IS AT HAND.` · `METANOIA — A CHANGE OF MIND.` · `A KING IS COMING. FIX THE ROAD.` · `HE POINTS AWAY FROM HIMSELF.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let one thing come to mind that you'd like to turn from: a habit that keeps the road crooked, a sharp way of talking, a grudge you keep feeding. Name it plainly, inside, without trying to fix it yet. If you pray, hold it up to God and ask for help turning; if you don't, just sit with the naming.
Metanoia. Greek for a change of mind, a turning around: John's call at the Jordan.
Your line: make straight the way. The road John meant runs through a life. Thirty-one days in.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John the Baptist's call in the Advent Sunday readings and answer it in the sacrament of penance (confession), where a person names their sins, receives absolution and is given a penance.

original.note: Greek: a change of mind, a turning around. The Latin Bible rendered John's call as do penance.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wild man in the desert telling people they're bad.
what it means: a voice clearing the road, calling people to turn around because someone greater is coming.
what a scholar hears: metanoia, a change of mind. the Latin paenitentiam agite, do penance, gave the Douay-Rheims its wording and the sacrament its old name.

notes: Quotations of Matthew 3:2 and 3:3 are given from the Challoner Douay-Rheims from memory; confirm wording and punctuation.
The carry 'make straight the way' matches John 1:23 ('make straight the way of the Lord'); Matthew 3:3 in Douay-Rheims reads 'make straight his paths'. Both are used; confirm.
Metanoia etymology (meta + nous) and the Vulgate 'paenitentiam agite' as the source of 'do penance': confirm, and confirm the link to the name 'sacrament of penance' is fairly stated.
'Fruit worthy of penance' (3:8) and 'not worthy to bear his shoes' (3:11) are paraphrased, not quoted.
Feasts: Nativity of John the Baptist June 24 (solemnity), Passion/Beheading August 29. Stated as 'one of very few saints whose birth has its own feast' (with Mary and Jesus); confirm phrasing.
Softened: the script now says the Latin wording is 'one reason' for the name 'sacrament of penance', not its sole source.
Dating of Isaiah 40: many scholars date Isaiah 40–55 to the sixth century BC (the exile). The script says only 'centuries earlier'.
Editor review (2026-10-01): the road-crew picture is now Isaiah's own image (40:4) rather than unsourced history; cut 'one of very few saints' and 'walking for hours'.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
